title: Monsoon to withdraw from Delhi, Punjab within 48 hours; more rain likely in several states - thehawk.in
article_text:
New Delhi, Oct 2 (IANS) The monsoon is expected to withdraw from the plains of North India, including Delhi, Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh, within the next 48 hours. However, the withdrawal is likely to be accompanied by another spell of rainfall in several parts of the country. Indian market trends
According to the Meteorological Department, rainfall is likely in Haryana, Chandigarh, Delhi and Punjab on October 6 and 7. Heavy rainfall is expected in Himachal Pradesh from October 5 to 7, Jammu and Kashmir from October 6 to 7, and Uttarakhand from October 5 to 7. Thunderstorms and gusty winds are also likely over Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand during this period.
Rainfall is expected to continue over Madhya Pradesh until October 3, while Chhattisgarh is likely to receive rain from October 2 to 7. Bihar and Jharkhand may also witness rainfall between October 5 and 7.
In the Northeast, monsoon activity has persisted around Imphal, the capital of Manipur. Rainfall is expected to continue in Meghalaya, Assam, Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh. Overall, rainfall activity is likely to remain subdued across most parts of the country between October 1 and 7.
However, isolated heavy rainfall is likely over Kerala, coastal Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and parts of the Northeast. Rainfall activity is expected to decline further during the second week of October. A fresh low-pressure area may, however, develop over the Andaman Sea around October 13.
The Meteorological Department has said the monsoon is likely to completely withdraw from eastern Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and the remaining parts of Haryana during the first week of October. Between October 8 and 14, the monsoon is expected to withdraw from Bihar, West Bengal, Jharkhand and the northeastern region as well.
Following the withdrawal from Delhi and Uttar Pradesh in the first week of October, monsoon activity is also expected to end over Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Gujarat by the second week.
The department has forecast post-monsoon rainfall between October and December. During these three months, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal, coastal Andhra Pradesh and Yanam, Rayalaseema, Kerala and Mahe, and south interior Karnataka are expected to receive rainfall. Overall rainfall during the post-monsoon season is most likely to remain between 88 and 112 per cent of the long-period average.
Except for the southern peninsula and parts of northwest India, most parts of the country are expected to receive below-normal rainfall during the post-monsoon period.
The four-month southwest monsoon season from June to September recorded average rainfall of around 87 per cent, which is below normal. The season witnessed spells of heavy rainfall interspersed with periods of deficient rainfall.
Central India, including Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh, received around 97 per cent of its normal rainfall, while northwest India, including Delhi and Uttar Pradesh, recorded around 94 per cent. In comparison, the southern peninsula and Northeast India received only around 76 per cent and 74 per cent of their normal rainfall, respectively.
The rainfall figures could have been lower without the heavy showers recorded during August and September. A deep depression that formed over Andhra Pradesh in late September brought significant rainfall to several regions, including Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Haryana, as well as Odisha, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh.
Between September 24 and 27, heavy rainfall was recorded in several areas of Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand. On September 28, another deep depression formed over the Andaman Sea and adjoining Myanmar coast, contributing to continued rainfall activity in parts of the country.

title: PDMA’s report on monsoon: 65 people died and 382 injured, whereas 224 houses damaged - Dawn
article_text:
LAHORE: Monsoon rains left 65 people dead and 382 injured across Punjab this year, besides damaging 224 houses and killing 21 livestock, according to a Provincial Disaster Management Authority (PDMA) report released as the monsoon season concluded on Thursday.

Most districts received exceptionally high rainfall during the season, with Rawalpindi recording the highest total of 1,505 millimetres, the report said.

The rains also triggered a flood-like situation in parts of Sheikhupura district, where overflowing Nullah Bhed and Nullah Dek inundated 58 villages in Ferozewala and Muridke.

The flooding affected 83 revenue estates and 43,188 acres of land.

The PDMA spokesperson said measures were being taken to provide compensation for crop and housing losses caused by the flooding in Sheikhupura. Affected families would also be compensated for losses under the Punjab government’s policy, the spokesperson added.

The total rainfall in three major cities was also exceptionally high, with Rawalpindi receiving 1,505mm during the monsoon, Lahore 1,316mm and Sialkot 1,256mm. Gujranwala recorded 1,161mm, while Jhelum received 935mm, Gujrat 865mm, Mandi Bahauddin 810mm, Narowal 786mm, Murree 757mm, Attock 749mm, Wazirabad 741mm and Mangla 602mm.

Other rainfall totals recorded by the PDMA included 576mm in Okara, 524mm in Sargodha, 514mm in Faisalabad, 422mm in Sheikhupura, 402mm in Chakwal, 388mm in Hafizabad, 307mm in Kasur, 293mm in Nankana Sahib, 276mm in Bahawalnagar, 265mm in Noorpur Thal, 247mm in Mianwali, 236mm in Khushab and 197mm in Toba Tek Singh.

Rainfall was also recorded in Jhang, Chiniot, Jauharabad, Sahiwal, Pakpattan, Bahawalpur, Khanewal, Multan, Kot Addu, Dera Ghazi Khan, Rahim Yar Khan, Rajanpur and Vehari.

The report said Punjab did not experience major flooding in any of its rivers during the monsoon, although rising water levels in drains in Sheikhupura created a flood-like situation.

PDMA Director General Muhammad Saif Anwer Jappa said timely drainage of rainwater had been ensured despite the record-breaking rainfall.

He said that proactive arrangements were made for drainage operation and machinery was also provided on time.

He said that the injured had been provided medical treatment and measures would be taken to compensate families affected by deaths, injuries and damage to property and livestock.

The PDMA said continuous monitoring of rivers, dams and barrages was being carried out and water flows in all rivers of Punjab remained normal. A 24/7 monitoring system was also maintained at the PDMA control room, the report said.

Mr Jappa said the authority, in coordination with relevant departments, remained prepared to deal with emergencies and had taken measures throughout the monsoon to respond to rain-related incidents.

Published in Dawn, October 2nd, 2026

title: Pune Monsoon Withdrawal May Come Early, IMD Says - urbanacres.in
article_text:
Pune could see the southwest monsoon withdraw earlier than usual as dry air enters Maharashtra and rainfall activity remains subdued, with the India Meteorological Department indicating that withdrawal from the state may begin within the next 24 to 48 hours.

The timing would be close to Maharashtra’s normal monsoon withdrawal commencement around October 4-5. Pune’s normal withdrawal window is later, around October 9-10, but the city may experience an early exit if dry conditions persist, IMD officials told the Times of India.

“There is no rain forecast for Pune from Friday,” an IMD official said. The department’s Pune forecast indicated mainly cloudy conditions initially, followed by partly cloudy skies and only a low likelihood of light rain. Officials said greater clarity on Pune’s withdrawal would emerge as the region approaches its normal withdrawal window.

The IMD uses more than a single dry day to declare the retreat of the monsoon. IMD scientist SD Sanap said rainfall must remain absent for consecutive days, while the prevailing southwesterly monsoon winds must weaken or reverse. “The main thing is rainfall. It should not rain for consecutive two to three days,” Sanap said.

An anticyclonic circulation over Rajasthan and adjoining areas is currently helping push dry air into Maharashtra. Sanap said the outflow from this circulation was causing dry-air intrusion over parts of the state and indicated that weather conditions across much of Maharashtra were likely to remain dry.

Rainfall conditions over north Madhya Maharashtra during the next 24 to 48 hours will be important in determining whether the withdrawal process begins, officials said. At present, the IMD has found no indication of a broad rainfall revival in parts of the state, allowing the possibility of withdrawal to remain open.

The emerging transition follows a prolonged lack of sustained moisture over Maharashtra during August and September. Independent weather expert Abhijit Modak attributed the subdued rainfall activity during those months to the movement of Bay of Bengal systems along tracks that did not support sustained moisture transport into the state.

Modak said September climatology often brings one or two lower-latitude Bay of Bengal systems westward from Andhra Pradesh and Telangana towards Marathwada, Nashik and north Konkan. Such systems can carry moisture into Maharashtra. This year, however, a system around September 10 moved from Odisha towards Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat, while another system that intensified after affecting Andhra Pradesh and Telangana curved northwards towards Chhattisgarh and Uttar Pradesh instead of continuing westward into Maharashtra.

For Pune, the immediate forecast is therefore one of mostly dry weather, although the IMD has not yet formally declared the monsoon withdrawn from the city. The department’s assessment over the next two to three days, including rainfall and wind conditions, will determine whether the early-exit possibility becomes an official withdrawal.

आज कैसा रहेगा मौसम? (CG Me Aaj Kaha Barish Hogi)

मौसम विभाग के मुताबिक दक्षिण-पश्चिम मानसून की वापसी की रेखा आगे बढ़ रही है, वहीं उत्तर-पश्चिम और उससे लगे पश्चिम-मध्य बंगाल की खाड़ी पर साइक्लोन सर्कुलेशन बना हुआ है। जिससे आने वाले दिनों में प्रदेश में बारिश की कोई संभावना नहीं है। मौसम वैज्ञानिकों ने बताया कि आज से 5 अक्टूबर तक छत्तीसगढ़ (Chhattisgarh Weather Update Today) के किसी भी जिले में कोई चेतावनी जारी नहीं की गई है। अगर बात करें राजधानी रायपुर (Raipur Weather Today) की तो यहां बारिश की कोई संभावना नहीं है, मौसम साफ रहेगा। मौसम विभाग ने अधिकतम तापमान करीब 34 डिग्री और न्यूनतम 25 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहने का अनुमान जताया है. बारिश की फिलहाल कोई संभावना नहीं है।

title: Northeast Monsoon Rainfall Hits Record Low Since 1901 - urbanacres.in
article_text:
The 2026 southwest monsoon has left east and northeast India with its lowest seasonal rainfall since 1901, according to the India Meteorological Department, turning what is usually one of the country’s wettest regions into the zone with the sharpest rainfall deficit. The outcome is significant not only because of the scale of the shortfall, but because the monsoon remains central to agriculture, water supply and economic activity across states where seasonal rainfall is a foundational part of the urban and rural economy.

The IMD said rainfall in east and northeast India totalled 1,017.1 mm during the June-to-September season, 26% below the region’s long-period average. The region received only 74% of its long-period average, the steepest departure among India’s four broad geographical zones. The South Peninsula also recorded a substantial shortfall, receiving 542.0 mm, its fourth-lowest monsoon rainfall since 1901 and second-lowest since 2001.

The national monsoon outcome was deficient as well, with the seasonal total falling below 90% of the long-period average. But the regional pattern was uneven. Central India received 94-106% of its long-period average, while northwest India recorded 92-108%. In contrast, east and northeast India recorded a 26% deficit and the South Peninsula a 24% deficit. The gap between these zones is important because national rainfall totals can conceal the localised pressure created when a particular region receives substantially less rain than its normal seasonal requirement.

Within the northeast, the deficit was especially severe in Meghalaya, which received 60% less rainfall than normal. Manipur recorded a 45% shortfall, Arunachal Pradesh 44% and Assam 28%. All four states were classified as deficient. Nagaland and Sikkim were exceptions: Nagaland recorded rainfall 6% above normal, while Sikkim received 10% more than its long-period average and recorded normal to above-normal seasonal rainfall.

This state-level spread shows why a regional rainfall average is an incomplete measure of water stress. The northeast is often treated as a single high-rainfall landscape, but the IMD figures show that its seasonal experience in 2026 varied sharply between states. A surplus in Nagaland or Sikkim did not offset the deficits in Meghalaya, Manipur, Arunachal Pradesh and Assam, particularly where communities and economic activities depend on the timing and distribution of rainfall rather than only on the national or regional total.

The urban implications begin with water systems. The supplied IMD assessment identifies water supply as one of the activities heavily dependent on the southwest monsoon in the northeast. Lower seasonal rainfall can therefore affect the replenishment of sources used by towns and cities, even though the available material does not quantify reservoir levels, groundwater conditions, municipal supply reductions or household-level shortages. Those indicators will be necessary to establish how the rainfall deficit is translating into direct urban stress.

For cities in Assam and the wider northeastern region, the rainfall figures also complicate the usual understanding of climate risk. Urban resilience is often discussed primarily through flooding, drainage capacity and extreme rainfall. A deficient monsoon introduces a different pressure: the need to maintain reliable water access and agricultural supply when the season delivers less rain than expected. The same region can therefore face intense rainfall events at particular times while still ending the season with a substantial overall deficit. The IMD data supplied here does not provide an event-by-event breakdown, but it establishes that seasonal scarcity and short-duration rainfall risk should not be treated as opposites.

The agricultural consequences are similarly important. The IMD states that the northeast relies heavily on the southwest monsoon for agriculture, water supply and other economic activities. A 60% shortfall in Meghalaya, a 45% deficit in Manipur, a 44% deficit in Arunachal Pradesh and a 28% deficit in Assam indicate that the pressure was not confined to one state or one type of landscape. However, the supplied report does not provide crop-wise losses, sowing data, irrigation coverage, reservoir storage or farm-income estimates. Those omissions matter because rainfall departure alone cannot show the full economic effect without information on when the rain fell and which sectors were exposed.

The season also highlights the limits of forecast-based planning when the eventual regional pattern diverges from the initial expectation. On May 29, the IMD forecast normal rainfall for the northeast, at 94-106% of the long-period average. The actual outcome was a 26% deficit. At the same time, the May forecast had projected below-normal rainfall for central, southern peninsular and northwestern India, yet central and northwest India ultimately recorded rainfall within their respective normal ranges, while the South Peninsula remained deficient.

This divergence does not by itself establish that the forecast was inadequate. Seasonal forecasts describe probabilities and broad patterns, while local impacts depend on rainfall timing, distribution and the performance of shorter-term weather systems. But it does show why public agencies cannot treat a seasonal outlook as a substitute for continuous monitoring. Water managers, municipal authorities and agriculture departments need to compare forecast signals with actual rainfall as the season develops, particularly in regions where water supply and livelihoods are strongly monsoon-dependent.

Institutionally, the rainfall numbers point to a coordination challenge. The IMD provides the seasonal assessment and regional departures, but the consequences are managed through several systems: municipal water supply, state water resources departments, agriculture agencies and local administrations. The supplied material does not identify any specific response measures, funding decisions or emergency plans following the 2026 deficit. That makes the next stage of scrutiny important: whether authorities publish information on water availability, agricultural impacts and local preparedness, and whether those responses are organised around state-level conditions rather than a single northeast-wide average.

The contrast between the four broad zones also raises a data and governance issue. India’s national monsoon total was deficient, but central and northwest India remained within their respective normal ranges. A national figure can therefore provide an important overview without adequately representing the exposure of individual states or cities. For urban planning, the more useful questions concern the reliability of local sources, the condition of distribution networks, the dependence on seasonal recharge and the capacity of administrations to respond when rainfall falls below normal.

The available evidence confirms three facts. East and northeast India experienced its lowest monsoon rainfall since 1901; the region’s 26% deficit was the country’s sharpest among the four broad zones; and the most severe state-level shortfalls occurred in Meghalaya, Manipur, Arunachal Pradesh and Assam. It also confirms a marked difference between the IMD’s May forecast for normal northeast rainfall and the eventual seasonal result. What remains unestablished in the supplied material is the precise effect on reservoirs, groundwater, municipal supply, crops, household access and local economies. Those measures will determine how a record rainfall deficit translates into an urban and regional water crisis, and they are the indicators that authorities and residents will need to watch after the monsoon ends.

title: Jharkhand Weather: मॉनसून की विदाई, 5-6 अक्टूबर को बारिश के आसार - 22Scope
article_text:
झारखंड से दक्षिण-पश्चिम मॉनसून की वापसी शुरू हो गई है। 5 और 6 अक्टूबर को कई इलाकों में बारिश के आसार हैं, जबकि तीन दिन बाद रात में गुलाबी ठंड महसूस होगी।

Jharkhand Weather रांची: झारखंड से दक्षिण-पश्चिम मॉनसून की विदाई की प्रक्रिया शुरू हो गई है। मौसम विज्ञान केंद्र के अनुसार, अगले 48 घंटे में मॉनसून के राज्य से पूरी तरह वापस होने की संभावना है। इसके साथ ही मौसम में बदलाव देखने को मिलेगा। 5 और 6 अक्टूबर को राज्य के कुछ हिस्सों में बादल छाने के साथ हल्की से मध्यम बारिश हो सकती है। वहीं, अगले तीन दिनों के बाद रात के तापमान में गिरावट के कारण गुलाबी ठंड का अहसास शुरू होने की संभावना है।

झारखंड समाचार

Jharkhand Weather:48 घंटे में झारखंड से विदा हो सकता है मॉनसून

मॉनसून की वापसी का असर झारखंड के साथ देश के कई राज्यों में भी दिखाई देगा। पंजाब, हरियाणा, राजस्थान, उत्तर प्रदेश के कुछ हिस्सों, गुजरात, मध्य प्रदेश, जम्मू-कश्मीर, हिमाचल प्रदेश, उत्तराखंड, बिहार के कुछ हिस्सों, छत्तीसगढ़ और महाराष्ट्र से भी दक्षिण-पश्चिम मॉनसून की वापसी की प्रक्रिया शुरू होने की संभावना है।

झारखंड में मॉनसून की वापसी के दौरान मौसम में उतार-चढ़ाव देखने को मिल सकता है। हालांकि, अधिकतम तापमान में फिलहाल बड़े बदलाव की संभावना नहीं है।

Jharkhand Weather:5 और 6 अक्टूबर को इन इलाकों में बारिश के आसार

मौसम विज्ञान केंद्र के अनुसार, 5 अक्टूबर को उत्तर-पूर्वी झारखंड में आंशिक रूप से बादल छाए रह सकते हैं। इस दौरान कुछ स्थानों पर हल्की बारिश होने की संभावना है।

6 अक्टूबर को उत्तर-पूर्वी और दक्षिण-पूर्वी झारखंड में मौसम बदलेगा। इन इलाकों में बादल छाए रहने के साथ कहीं-कहीं हल्की से मध्यम बारिश और मेघ गर्जन की संभावना जताई गई है। इसके बाद अन्य दिनों में राज्य में मौसम मुख्य रूप से शुष्क रहने का अनुमान है।

Key Highlights

झारखंड से दक्षिण-पश्चिम मॉनसून की वापसी शुरू हो गई है। अगले 48 घंटे में राज्य से मॉनसून की पूरी तरह वापसी संभव है। 5 अक्टूबर को उत्तर-पूर्वी झारखंड में हल्की बारिश के आसार हैं। 6 अक्टूबर को उत्तर-पूर्वी और दक्षिण-पूर्वी हिस्सों में बारिश और मेघ गर्जन की संभावना है। तीन दिनों बाद रात में गुलाबी ठंड महसूस होने की संभावना है।

Jharkhand Weather:रांची में 29.4 डिग्री रहा अधिकतम तापमान

रांची में गुरुवार को अधिकतम तापमान 29.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया, जबकि न्यूनतम तापमान 19.8 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा। अधिकतम तापमान में 0.2 डिग्री और न्यूनतम तापमान में 0.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस की कमी दर्ज की गई। मौसम में बदलाव और रात के तापमान में संभावित गिरावट के कारण अगले तीन दिनों के बाद रांची समेत झारखंड के कई हिस्सों में गुलाबी ठंड का अहसास शुरू हो सकता है। वहीं, मेदिनीनगर में गुरुवार को अधिकतम तापमान 33.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया।

title: SW Monsoon 2026: District wise rainfall in India - sandrp.in
article_text:
SW Monsoon 2026: District wise rainfall in India
RAINFALL
SW Monsoon 2026: District wise rainfall in India
October 2, 2026SANDRP

In the just concluded South West Monsoon 2026, India received 759.4 mm (937.2 mm in SW Monsoon 2025, 934.8 mm in SW Monsoon 2024, 820 mm in SW Monsoon 2023, 925 mm in SW Monsoon 2022[i]) rainfall, about 87.4% (107.9% in 2025, 107.6% in 2024, 94.45 % in 2023, 106.5% in 2022) of the Normal SW Monsoon rainfall of 868.6 mm as per India Meteorological Department (IMD). The 2026 SW Monsoon rainfall is 4th lowest since 2001 and first deficient monsoon since 2015. It is the 13th lowest rainfall since 1901. This rainfall is categorised as deficient rainfall since deficit is over 10%.  

In SW Monsoon 2021, the rainfall was 874.6 mm, 0.68% below normal rainfall. In SW Monsoon 2020, the rainfall was 956.7 mm, or about 8.74% above normal and in SW Monsoon 2019 it was 10.4% above normal.

Monsoon has yet to withdraw from India till Sept 30, when IMD closes its SW Monsoon record books. The monsoon after 8 am on Sept 30 will be counted in post monsoon rainfall. The monsoon is likely to take another couple of weeks to withdraw from the country and this may also delay the onset of NE Monsoon, that is active mainly in some parts of South India. The NE Monsoon onset is likely after Oct 15 2026.

Monthly Rainfall The Month wise rainfall during the SW Monsoon 2026 was as follows.

Month	Actual Rainfall, mm	Normal Rainfall, mm	% Departure
June	99.5	165.3	60.2
July	290.3	280.5	103.5
Aug	213.9	254.9	83.9
Sept	155.7	167.9	92.7
SW Monsoon 2026	759.4	868.6	87.4

Need for an index of rainfall distribution spatially and temporally As we can see from the table above, the rainfall varied from over 39.8% below normal in Jun to 3.5% above normal in July. There has been even wider variation spatially and temporally, but we do not have an index of rainfall distribution over time and space that captures these variations. What we need is an index of rainfall that will not only capture the quantum of rainfall as it does today, but also the temporal and spatial distribution of rainfall across the monsoon and across the nation or states. This will give a better picture of the monsoon rainfall and would also help us understand how this index is changing.

Daily National Rainfall Bar Chart The bar chart above is for the Daily National Rainfall figure for the SW monsoon period from June 1 to Sep 30 2026. Regional rainfall figures for SW Monsoon 2026 is given in table below.

Region	Actual Rainfall, mm	Normal Rainfall, mm	% Departure
E & NE India	1017.1	1367.3	-26
NW India	553	587.6	-6
Central India	952.8	978	-3
South Peninsula	542	716.2	-24

State wise Rainfall As we can see from the IMD map above, in the four month long South West Monsoon 2026, out of 36 States and Union Territories (UTs), One (Ladakh) had Large Excess, Two (Odisha and Dadra-Nagarhaveli-Diu-Daman) had Excess (Actual rainfall 20-59% above normal), 18 had normal (Actual rainfall 19% below normal to 19% above normal), 14 had deficit (Actual rainfall 20-59% below normal rainfall) and one (Meghalaya) had Large Deficit (Actual rainfall over 60% below normal) in rainfall. Ladakh had the lowest rainfall (like in 2022-2025) at 49.4 mm and highest surplus at 122%. Diu-Daman-Dadra-Nagarhaveli had the highest rainfall at 3000.1 mm.  

Sub Division wise rainfall IMD divides India into 36 meteorological divisions (the logic of many of them is questionable). As we can see from the IMD map of Sub Division wise rainfall above of SW Monsoon 2026, NO sub division had Large Excess rainfall, One (Odisha) sub division had excess rainfall, 18 had Normal rainfall and 17 had deficit rainfall. Coastal Konkan and Goa had the highest rainfall at 2453 mm and W Rajasthan had the lowest at 198.8 mm rainfall. Odisha had the highest surplus rainfall % at 29%. Assam-Meghalaya had the highest deficit rainfall % at 44%.

All India District wise rainfall departure map The map above provides district wise picture of rainfall at all India level.

DISTRICT WISE STATE WISE RAINFALL The maps below are from IMD, showing in colour code the district wise rainfall situation for states and UTs during SW Monsoon 2026.

Meghalaya had the highest rainfall deficit throughout SW Monsoon 2026 Meghalaya is facing its highest-ever monsoon rainfall deficit in 2026 and 10 of 11 districts classified as deficient or largely deficient. This emerging drought-like situation threatens agriculture, water security, and spring-fed drinking supplies, compounding long-term trends of declining monsoon rainfall and climate stress.

A 30 year (1989-2018) analysis of monsoon rainfall data in Meghalaya by the IMD showed a significant decreasing trend in monsoon rainfall during the period.

Karnataka stares at worst drought in 150 years Karnataka has recorded its worst southwest monsoon rainfall deficit in 55 years, with rainfall from June 1 to Sept 30 falling 35% below normal, according to data from Karnataka State Natural Disaster Monitoring Centre (KSNDMC). The deficit is the lowest recorded since 1971, surpassing the previous low of 33% in 2002.


The state received just 551 mm of rainfall against the normal 852 mm during the four-month monsoon season. While rainfall improved in July and August, September saw a sharp reversal, with the state recording a 54% deficit during the month. According to KSNDMC data, in June 2026, the state recorded -42% deficit rainfall, which improved to -29% in July. In Aug, due to further improvement in rainfall, the deficit fell to -23%.

North interior Karnataka is the worst affected with -42% deficit rainfall, followed by south interior Karnataka, which recorded -41% deficit rainfall. Malnad region, comprising the four districts of Kodagu, Shivamogga, Hassan, and Chikkamagaluru recorded -38% deficit rainfall. The coastal region recorded -28% deficit rainfall.

Of the 31 revenue districts, Mysuru was the worst affected, with a 59% deficit, followed by Vijayanagara at 57%. Only Bengaluru South recorded rainfall within the normal range, with a deficit of 18%. Against normal rainfall of 419 mm, Mysuru received just 172 mm.

title: Odisha Weather Alert: Depression Weakens, Thunderstorm Warning Issued - Pragativadi
article_text:
A persistent weather depression centred over northeast Madhya Pradesh and adjoining north Chhattisgarh continues its north-northwestward journey, bringing heavy precipitation across central and eastern India.

While the system is expected to lose intensity over the next 12 to 24 hours, meteorologists have sounded a high alert for Odisha, where intense rainfall and thunderstorms threaten multiple districts.

Depression Trajectory & Weakening Forecast

Moving at a speed of 13 km/h over the past six hours, the depression was centred near latitude 23.8°N and longitude 81.6°E.

The system lies approximately:

70 km south-southwest of Sidhi (MP)

90 km south-southeast of Rewa (MP)

120 km southeast of Satna (MP)

180 km south of Prayagraj (UP)

250 km south-southeast of Fatehpur (UP)

According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), the depression will maintain its current intensity as it moves across northeast Madhya Pradesh toward southeast Uttar Pradesh. It is projected to gradually weaken into a well-marked low-pressure area during the subsequent 12 hours. Radar stations at Raipur and Lucknow are continuously monitoring the system’s trajectory.

Torrential Downpours Inundate Odisha

Even as the atmospheric depression shifts away, its trailing arm has triggered widespread heavy to very heavy rainfall across eastern India. Odisha recorded intense precipitation at 19 key locations across nine districts during the 24-hour period ending Saturday morning.

Location District Recorded Rainfall Rainfall Category Nawana Mayurbhanj 126 mm Very Heavy Rainfall Raighar Nabarangpur 107 mm Heavy Rainfall Khaira Baleshwar 101 mm Heavy Rainfall

Thunderstorm & Safety Warnings Issued

The regional weather office has extended a thunderstorm warning valid until Sunday morning, cautioning residents against short-duration, high-intensity lightning and gusty winds.

Alerted Districts: Kendujhar, Mayurbhanj, Baleshwar, Bhadrak, Jajpur, Sundaragada, Jagatsinghpur, Kendrapada, Khordha, Kataka, Puri, Nayagada, Anugola, Dhenkanal, and Debagada.

Disaster management authorities have advised residents in the designated districts to avoid sheltering under trees or near untethered structures during lightning strikes and to monitor official advisories closely.

title: ગુજરાતમાં 6 ઓગસ્ટ સુધી ભારે વરસાદના એંધાણ, જાણો તમારા જિલ્લાની આગાહી - Mumbai Samachar
article_text:
Mumbai Samachar
/
gujarat

ગુજરાતમાં 6 ઓગસ્ટ સુધી ભારે વરસાદના એંધાણ, જાણો તમારા જિલ્લાની આગાહી
2026-08-01 09:02:00
Author: Mayur Patel



અમદાવાદઃ રાજ્યમાં વરસાદના ત્રીજા રાઉન્ડની ધમાકેદાર શરૂઆત થઈ છે. હવામાન વિભાગ દ્વારા 6 ઓગસ્ટ સુધીનું પૂર્વાનુમાન જાહેર કરવામાં આવ્યું હતું.  આજે હવામાન વિભાગે અમદાવાદ, આણંદ, સુરેન્દ્રનગર, રાજકોટ, બોટાદ અને ભાવનગર જિલ્લામાં વરસાદનું રેડ એલર્ટ આપ્યું છે. જ્યારે કચ્છ, અમરેલી, ભરૂચ, પાટણ, ગાંધીનગર, વાવ થરાદ, મહેસાણા, સાબરકાંઠા, મોરબી, અરવલ્લી ઓરેન્જ એલર્ટ તથા  દેવભૂમિ દ્વારકા, પોરબંદર, જામનગર, જૂનાગઢ, ખેડા, વડોદરા, સુરત, પંચમહાલ, મહીસાગર, દાહોદ, દીવ, દમણ અને દાદરા નગર હવેલીમાં યલો એલર્ટ જાહેર કરવામાં આવ્યું છે. 

આવતીકાલે કયા જિલ્લામાં પડશે ભારે વરસાદ

2 ઓગસ્ટના રોજ મોટાભાગના જિલ્લાઓમાં વરસાદનું જોર ઘટશે, પરંતુ પવનના સુસવાટા સાથે વરસાદ રહેશે. બનાસકાંઠા, પાટણ, મહેસાણા, સાબરકાંઠા, મોરબી અને કચ્છ જિલ્લામાં છૂટાછવાયા સ્થળોએ ભારે વરસાદની શક્યતા છે. ગાંધીનગર, અરવલ્લી, ખેડા, અમદાવાદ, આણંદ, પંચમહાલ, દાહોદ, મહીસાગર, વડોદરા, છોટા ઉદેપુર, નર્મદા, ભરૂચ, સુરત, ડાંગ, નવસારી, વલસાડ, તાપી, દમણ, દાદરા અને નગર હવેલી, સુરેન્દ્રનગર, રાજકોટ, જામનગર, પોરબંદર, જૂનાગઢ, અમરેલી, ભાવનગર, દેવભૂમિ દ્વારકા, ગીર સોમનાથ, બોટાદ અને દીવમાં 40 થી 50 કિમી પ્રતિ કલાકની ઝડપે ફૂંકાતા પવન અને હળવી મેઘગર્જના સાથે હળવાથી મધ્યમ વરસાદની સંભાવના છે.


3 ઓગસ્ટે રાજ્યના મોટાભાગના જિલ્લાઓમાં અમુક સ્થળોએ ગાજવીજ સાથે હળવાથી મધ્યમ વરસાદની શક્યતા છે. જ્યારે 4 થી 6 ઓગસ્ટ બનાસકાંઠા, પાટણ, મહેસાણા, સાબરકાંઠા, ગાંધીનગર, અરવલ્લી, ખેડા, અમદાવાદ, પંચમહાલ, દાહોદ, મહીસાગર, વડોદરા, છોટા ઉદેપુર, નર્મદા, ભરૂચ, સુરત, ડાંગ, નવસારી, વલસાડ, તાપી, રાજકોટ, જામનગર, પોરબંદર, જૂનાગઢ, અમરેલી, ભાવનગર, મોરબી, દ્વારકા, ગીર સોમનાથ, બોટાદ, દીવ અને કચ્છના છૂટાછવાયા વિસ્તારોમાં ગાજવીજ સાથે હળવાથી મધ્યમ વરસાદી છાંટા કે ઝાપટાં પડવાની શક્યતા છે. 


રાજ્યમાં છેલ્લા 24 કલાકમાં કેટલો વરસાદ નોંધાયો

સ્ટેટ ઈમરજન્સી ઓપરેશન સેન્ટર, ગાંધીનગર દ્વારા જાહેર કરવામાં આવેલા આંકડા મુજબ આજે સવારે 6 કલાકે પૂરા થયેલા છેલ્લા 24 કલાકમાં  255 તાલુકામાં વરસાદ પડ્યો હતો. એક તાલુકામાં 24 ઇંચથી વધારે, ત્રણ તાલુકામાં 16 ઇંચથી વધારે, ત્રણ તાલુકામાં 13 ઇંચથી વધારે, છ તાલુકામાં 10 ઇંચથી વધારે વરસાદ ખાબક્યો હતો.  

પાંચ તાલુકામાં 9 ઇંચથી વધારે, છ તાલુકામાં 8 ઇંચથી વધારે, છ તાલુકામાં 7 ઇંચથી વધારે, 12 તાલુકામાં 6 ઇંચથી વધારે, 20 તાલુકામાં 5 ઇંચથી વધારે, 11 તાલુકામાં 4 ઇંચથી વધારે,  25 તાલુકામાં 3 ઇંચથી વધારે, 48 તાલુકામાં 2 ઇંચથી વધારે,  39 તાલુકામાં 1 ઇંચથી વધારે અને 72 તાલુકામાં એક ઇંચથી વધારે વરસાદ નોંધાયો હતો. સુરતના અંબિકામાં સૌથી વધુ 24.06 ઇંચ, તાપીના ડોલવણમાં 16.73 ઇંચ, ખેડાના વસોમાં 16.38 ઇંચ, નવસારીના વાંસદામાં 16.26 ઇંચ, સુરતના ઉમરપાડામાં 14.69 ઇંચ, ખેડાના નડીયાદમાં 13.43 ઇંચ, ભરૂચના નેત્રંગમાં 13.03 ઇંચ, વલસાડના ધરમપુરમાં 11.02 ઇંચ, ડાંગના વઘાઈમાં 10.94 ઇંચ, સુરતના માંગરોળમાં 10.71 ઇંચ, આણંદમાં 10.67 ઇંચ, ડાંગના સુબીરમાં 10.24 ઇંચ, આણંદના ખંભાતમાં 10.16 ઇંચ વરસાદ ખાબક્યો હતો.
